title: Structure and Bonding

source.note: Facts are paraphrased from the Chapter 1 source text for flashcard and explorer use.

chapter_goals: Connect atomic structure and electron configuration to ordinary organic bonding patterns.
Use valence bond hybridization to predict molecular geometry around carbon and common heteroatoms.
Distinguish sigma, pi, bonding molecular orbital, and antibonding molecular orbital descriptions.
Translate among Lewis, line-bond, condensed, and skeletal organic structures.

visual_requirements.description: Methane with four equivalent C-H bonds arranged tetrahedrally and annotated 109.5 deg H-C-H angles.
One s orbital plus three p orbitals combining into four directional sp3 hybrid orbitals aimed at a tetrahedron.
Ethane showing sp3-sp3 sigma overlap for the C-C bond, six C-H sigma bonds, and free rotation around the C-C sigma bond.
Ethylene with planar sp2 geometry, 120 deg approximate bond angles, one sigma bond, and one pi bond above and below the C-C axis.
Acetylene with linear sp geometry, 180 deg H-C-C angles, one sigma bond, and two perpendicular pi bonds.
Molecular orbital diagram contrasting additive bonding and subtractive antibonding combinations for H2 and pi orbitals.
Line-angle drawing guide showing implied carbons at line ends/intersections, omitted carbon-bound hydrogens, and displayed heteroatoms.

sections.title: Atomic Structure: The Nucleus
sections.focus: Atomic particles, isotope notation, atomic weight, and organic-scale distances.
facts: An atom has a dense positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons at a comparatively large distance.
The nucleus contains positively charged protons and neutral neutrons; a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
The nucleus is tiny compared with the atom but contains essentially all of the atom's mass.
Atomic number Z counts protons; mass number A counts protons plus neutrons.
Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different mass numbers because they contain different numbers of neutrons.
Atomic weight is the abundance-weighted average mass of naturally occurring isotopes, reported in unified atomic mass units or daltons.
Typical atomic diameters are about 2 x 10^-10 m, or about 200 pm; 1 angstrom equals 100 pm.

candidate_cards.front: What does atomic number Z count?
candidate_cards.back: Atomic number Z counts the number of protons in the nucleus; in a neutral atom it also equals the number of electrons.

candidate_cards.front: How do isotopes of the same element differ?
candidate_cards.back: They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers.

candidate_cards.front: Same Z, different A.
candidate_cards.back: This describes isotopes: atoms of the same element with different mass numbers.

candidate_cards.front: Carbon-13 has atomic number 6. How many neutrons does it contain?
candidate_cards.back: 7 neutrons, because A = protons + neutrons, so 13 = 6 + neutrons.

candidate_cards.front: What does atomic weight average over?
candidate_cards.back: It averages the masses of naturally occurring isotopes according to their natural abundances.

sections.title: Atomic Structure: Orbitals
sections.focus: Wave functions, orbital shapes, shells, nodes, and p-orbital phase.
facts: A wave function, or orbital, describes where an electron is likely to be found around a nucleus.
The square of the wave function corresponds to electron probability density.
Orbitals are often drawn as regions containing most of the electron probability rather than as hard-edged objects.
An s orbital is spherical; a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped; most d orbitals are four-lobed.
Electron shells increase in size and energy as they get farther from the nucleus.
Each orbital can hold up to two electrons.
The first shell has one 1s orbital and holds 2 electrons; the second shell has 2s plus three 2p orbitals and holds 8 electrons.
The three p orbitals in a shell are mutually perpendicular and are commonly labeled px, py, and pz.
A p orbital has a node between its two lobes, and the two lobes have opposite algebraic signs in the wave function.

candidate_cards.front: In quantum terms, what is an orbital?
candidate_cards.back: An orbital is a wave function used to describe the region where an electron is likely to be found.

candidate_cards.front: What is the shape of an s orbital?
candidate_cards.back: An s orbital is spherical around the nucleus.

candidate_cards.front: What is the shape of a p orbital?
candidate_cards.back: A p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, with two lobes separated by a node.

candidate_cards.front: Compare the first and second electron shells by orbital contents and capacity.
candidate_cards.back: The first shell has one 1s orbital and holds 2 electrons. The second shell has one 2s and three 2p orbitals and holds 8 electrons.

candidate_cards.front: Diagram prompt: show the three 2p orbitals and the key feature that separates each pair of lobes.
candidate_cards.back: Draw px, py, and pz as mutually perpendicular dumbbells, each with a nodal plane between lobes and opposite signs on the two lobes.

sections.title: Atomic Structure: Electron Configurations
sections.focus: Ground-state configurations and the three filling rules.
facts: A ground-state electron configuration lists the occupied orbitals for the lowest-energy arrangement of an atom's electrons.
The Aufbau principle says electrons fill lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy orbitals.
The Pauli exclusion principle says an orbital can hold two electrons only if their spins are opposite.
Hund's rule says equal-energy empty orbitals receive one electron each with parallel spins before pairing begins.
Orbital superscripts indicate how many electrons occupy that orbital or subshell.
Carbon's ground-state valence pattern has four valence electrons, conventionally represented as 2s2 2p2.

candidate_cards.front: What is a ground-state electron configuration?
candidate_cards.back: It is the lowest-energy arrangement of an atom's electrons among available orbitals.

candidate_cards.front: What does the Aufbau principle say?
candidate_cards.back: Electrons occupy lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy orbitals.

candidate_cards.front: What does the Pauli exclusion principle say about one orbital?
candidate_cards.back: One orbital can hold at most two electrons, and if two are present they must have opposite spins.

candidate_cards.front: What does Hund's rule say about equal-energy orbitals?
candidate_cards.back: Place one electron in each equal-energy orbital with parallel spins before pairing electrons.

candidate_cards.front: Using normal valences, how many valence electrons does carbon bring to organic bonding?
candidate_cards.back: Carbon brings four valence electrons.

sections.title: Development of Chemical Bonding Theory
sections.focus: Tetravalent carbon, three-dimensional carbon geometry, ionic and covalent bonding, Lewis and Kekule structures.
facts: Carbon is tetravalent in stable organic compounds and can bond to itself to form chains and rings.
Tetrahedral carbon places four substituents toward the corners of a tetrahedron with carbon at the center.
Solid wedge/dash conventions encode three-dimensional geometry: ordinary lines are in the page, wedges project forward, and dashed bonds project backward.
Bond formation releases energy because the bonded product is lower in energy than the separated atoms.
Bond breaking absorbs energy.
Main-group atoms often react to reach a noble-gas-like valence shell.
Ionic bonds result from electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Covalent bonds result from sharing electron pairs between atoms; a neutral covalently bonded collection of atoms is a molecule.
Lewis structures show valence electrons as dots; line-bond, or Kekule, structures show each shared pair as a line.
Common neutral valences: H and halogens form 1 bond, O forms 2, N forms 3, C forms 4.

candidate_cards.front: What does tetravalent mean for carbon?
candidate_cards.back: A tetravalent carbon forms four covalent bonds in a stable neutral organic structure.

candidate_cards.front: What do wedge and dash bonds show?
candidate_cards.back: They show 3D orientation: a wedge points toward the viewer and a dashed bond points away from the viewer.

candidate_cards.front: How do ionic and covalent bonds differ?
candidate_cards.back: Ionic bonds are attractions between ions with opposite charges; covalent bonds share electron pairs between atoms.

candidate_cards.front: Does forming a bond release or absorb energy?
candidate_cards.back: Bond formation releases energy; bond breaking absorbs energy.

candidate_cards.front: Predict the typical number of covalent bonds for neutral C, N, O, H, and Cl.
candidate_cards.back: C forms 4, N forms 3, O forms 2, H forms 1, and Cl forms 1.

candidate_cards.front: A structure where each covalent electron pair is drawn as a line.
candidate_cards.back: That is a line-bond or Kekule structure.

sections.title: Describing Chemical Bonds: Valence Bond Theory
sections.focus: Orbital overlap, sigma bonds, bond strength, and bond length.
facts: Valence bond theory describes a covalent bond as overlap between singly occupied orbitals on two atoms.
The paired electrons in overlapping orbitals are attracted to both nuclei.
A sigma bond forms by head-on overlap along the internuclear axis.
A sigma bond has cylindrical symmetry around the line connecting the nuclei.
Bond strength is the energy needed to break a bond homolytically into separated atoms or fragments.
The H-H bond strength is about 436 kJ/mol and the H-H bond length is about 74 pm.
Bond length is the internuclear distance at minimum energy.

candidate_cards.front: In valence bond theory, when does a covalent bond form?
candidate_cards.back: When singly occupied orbitals on two atoms overlap and the paired electrons are attracted to both nuclei.

candidate_cards.front: What is a sigma bond?
candidate_cards.back: A sigma bond is formed by head-on orbital overlap along the line connecting two nuclei.

candidate_cards.front: What spatial symmetry does a sigma bond have?
candidate_cards.back: It has cylindrical symmetry around the internuclear axis.

candidate_cards.front: Distinguish bond strength from bond length.
candidate_cards.back: Bond strength is the energy needed to break the bond; bond length is the equilibrium distance between the bonded nuclei.

sections.title: sp3 Hybrid Orbitals and the Structure of Methane
sections.focus: sp3 hybridization, tetrahedral methane, and 109.5 degree bond angles.
facts: Hybridization combines atomic orbitals on the same atom into new directional hybrid orbitals.
One s orbital plus three p orbitals form four equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals.
The superscript in sp3 indicates that three p orbitals participate in the hybrid set.
The four sp3 orbitals point toward the corners of a tetrahedron.
sp3 orbitals are directional and asymmetric, so their larger lobes overlap effectively with other orbitals.
Methane has four equivalent C-H sigma bonds formed by overlap of carbon sp3 orbitals with hydrogen 1s orbitals.
Methane's H-C-H angle is 109.5 degrees.
Methane C-H bonds are about 109 pm long and about 439 kJ/mol strong.

candidate_cards.front: What atomic orbitals combine to make four sp3 hybrids?
candidate_cards.back: One s orbital and three p orbitals combine to form four equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals.

candidate_cards.front: What geometry and bond angle are associated with sp3 carbon in methane?
candidate_cards.back: Tetrahedral geometry with ideal H-C-H angles of 109.5 degrees.

candidate_cards.front: Diagram prompt: show how methane gets four equivalent C-H bonds.
candidate_cards.back: Show carbon with four sp3 hybrid orbitals pointing tetrahedrally, each overlapping with a hydrogen 1s orbital to make a C-H sigma bond.

candidate_cards.front: Four equivalent directional hybrids arranged toward the corners of a tetrahedron.
candidate_cards.back: This describes sp3 hybrid orbitals.

candidate_cards.front: A carbon has four single bonds and no pi bonds. What hybridization should you expect?
candidate_cards.back: sp3, with approximately tetrahedral geometry.

sections.title: sp3 Hybrid Orbitals and the Structure of Ethane
sections.focus: sp3-sp3 sigma bonding in carbon chains.
facts: Ethane is the simplest molecule containing a carbon-carbon bond.
The C-C bond in ethane forms by head-on overlap of an sp3 hybrid orbital from each carbon.
The remaining three sp3 orbitals on each carbon overlap with hydrogen 1s orbitals to make six C-H sigma bonds.
Ethane bond angles are near the tetrahedral value of 109.5 degrees.
The ethane C-C single bond is about 153 pm long and about 377 kJ/mol strong.
Rotation is possible around a simple C-C sigma bond because head-on overlap is cylindrically symmetric.

candidate_cards.front: How is the C-C bond in ethane formed?
candidate_cards.back: By head-on sigma overlap of one sp3 hybrid orbital from each carbon.

candidate_cards.front: How are the carbon orbitals in methane and ethane similar?
candidate_cards.back: Both use sp3 hybrid orbitals and have approximately tetrahedral bond angles around carbon.

candidate_cards.front: Diagram prompt: show the sigma-bond framework of ethane.
candidate_cards.back: Show an sp3-sp3 C-C sigma bond plus six C-H sigma bonds from carbon sp3 orbitals overlapping hydrogen 1s orbitals.

candidate_cards.front: Predict the approximate bond angle around each carbon in propane, CH3CH2CH3.
candidate_cards.back: Each carbon is sp3-hybridized, so the angles are approximately tetrahedral, near 109.5 degrees.

sections.title: sp2 Hybrid Orbitals and the Structure of Ethylene
sections.focus: Double bonds, trigonal planar geometry, and pi bonding.
facts: A carbon-carbon double bond shares two electron pairs.
One s orbital plus two p orbitals form three sp2 hybrid orbitals, leaving one unhybridized p orbital.
The three sp2 orbitals lie in a plane about 120 degrees apart.
In ethylene, the two carbons form a sigma bond by sp2-sp2 head-on overlap.
The unhybridized p orbitals on adjacent carbons overlap sideways to form a pi bond.
The pi bond places electron density above and below the internuclear axis.
Ethylene is planar, with bond angles close to 120 degrees.
The C-C double bond in ethylene is shorter and stronger than the C-C single bond in ethane.
A double bond is less than twice as strong as a single bond because pi overlap is weaker than sigma overlap.

candidate_cards.front: What orbitals form an sp2 hybrid set?
candidate_cards.back: One s orbital and two p orbitals form three sp2 hybrids, leaving one p orbital unhybridized.

candidate_cards.front: What two parts make up the C-C double bond in ethylene?
candidate_cards.back: One sp2-sp2 sigma bond and one pi bond from sideways overlap of unhybridized p orbitals.

candidate_cards.front: Compare ethane's C-C bond with ethylene's C-C bond.
candidate_cards.back: Ethane has a longer, weaker C-C single sigma bond. Ethylene has a shorter, stronger C-C double bond made from one sigma bond plus one pi bond.

candidate_cards.front: Diagram prompt: show the pi bond in ethylene.
candidate_cards.back: Draw planar sp2 carbons with the sigma bond on the C-C axis and p orbitals overlapping above and below the plane to make a pi bond.

candidate_cards.front: A carbon participates in one double bond and two single bonds. What hybridization and approximate geometry should you expect?
candidate_cards.back: sp2 hybridization with trigonal planar geometry and angles near 120 degrees.

sections.title: sp Hybrid Orbitals and the Structure of Acetylene
sections.focus: Triple bonds, linear geometry, and two perpendicular pi bonds.
facts: A carbon-carbon triple bond shares three electron pairs.
One s orbital plus one p orbital form two sp hybrid orbitals, leaving two unhybridized p orbitals.
The two sp orbitals point 180 degrees apart.
In acetylene, sp-sp head-on overlap forms one C-C sigma bond.
Two perpendicular pairs of unhybridized p orbitals overlap sideways to form two pi bonds.
Acetylene is linear with H-C-C angles of 180 degrees.
The C-C triple bond is shorter and stronger than carbon-carbon single and double bonds.

candidate_cards.front: What orbitals form an sp hybrid set?
candidate_cards.back: One s orbital and one p orbital form two sp hybrids, leaving two p orbitals unhybridized.

candidate_cards.front: What makes up the C-C triple bond in acetylene?
candidate_cards.back: One sp-sp sigma bond plus two perpendicular pi bonds from sideways p-p overlap.

candidate_cards.front: What geometry and bond angle are associated with sp carbon in acetylene?
candidate_cards.back: Linear geometry with 180 degree bond angles.

candidate_cards.front: Order C-C single, double, and triple bonds by length and strength.
candidate_cards.back: Length decreases and strength increases from single to double to triple: single is longest/weakest, triple is shortest/strongest.

candidate_cards.front: A carbon participates in one triple bond and one single bond. What hybridization should you expect?
candidate_cards.back: sp hybridization, with a linear arrangement around that carbon.

sections.title: Hybridization of Nitrogen, Oxygen, Phosphorus, and Sulfur
sections.focus: Hybridization and lone pairs on common heteroatoms.
facts: Hybridization is used to describe bonding in heteroatoms as well as carbon.
A neutral amine nitrogen is often described as sp3-hybridized, with three sigma bonds and one lone pair.
The lone pair on sp3 nitrogen occupies one of the four tetrahedral orbital directions and strongly affects reactivity.
An alcohol or ether oxygen is often described as sp3-hybridized, with two sigma bonds and two lone pairs.
Methanol has a C-O-H angle close to tetrahedral.
Phosphorus and sulfur are third-row analogs of nitrogen and oxygen, but they can form expanded-valence compounds.
Organophosphate phosphorus bonded to four oxygens is commonly treated as approximately sp3 with O-P-O angles near tetrahedral.
Thiols and sulfides can be described with approximate sp3 hybridization at sulfur, though their angles may deviate noticeably from 109.5 degrees.

candidate_cards.front: How is a neutral amine nitrogen commonly hybridized?
candidate_cards.back: It is commonly described as sp3, with three bonding orbitals and one lone-pair orbital.

candidate_cards.front: How is an alcohol or ether oxygen commonly hybridized?
candidate_cards.back: It is commonly described as sp3, with two sigma bonds and two lone pairs.

candidate_cards.front: Compare sp3 nitrogen in an amine with sp3 oxygen in an alcohol.
candidate_cards.back: Amine nitrogen usually has three bonds and one lone pair; alcohol oxygen usually has two bonds and two lone pairs.

candidate_cards.front: In CH3NH2, how many lone pairs are on nitrogen, and what hybridization is expected?
candidate_cards.back: Nitrogen has one lone pair and is expected to be approximately sp3-hybridized.

candidate_cards.front: In CH3OH, how many lone pairs are on oxygen, and what hybridization is expected?
candidate_cards.back: Oxygen has two lone pairs and is expected to be approximately sp3-hybridized.

sections.title: Describing Chemical Bonds: Molecular Orbital Theory
sections.focus: Molecular orbitals, bonding and antibonding combinations, and pi MO descriptions.
facts: Molecular orbital theory forms orbitals for the whole molecule by combining atomic orbitals mathematically.
A molecular orbital has a size, shape, and energy, just as an atomic orbital does.
Combining two atomic orbitals gives two molecular orbitals: one lower-energy bonding orbital and one higher-energy antibonding orbital.
An additive combination concentrates electron density between nuclei and is bonding.
A subtractive combination creates a node between nuclei and is antibonding.
For H2, two 1s atomic orbitals combine to give filled sigma bonding and empty sigma antibonding molecular orbitals.
For ethylene, sideways p-orbital combinations produce pi bonding and pi antibonding molecular orbitals.
Same-sign p lobes combine to make a lower-energy pi bonding MO; opposite-sign lobes combine to make a higher-energy pi antibonding MO.
MO theory is especially useful for pi systems involving more than one double bond.

candidate_cards.front: What is a molecular orbital?
candidate_cards.back: A molecular orbital is an orbital that belongs to the molecule as a whole and describes where electrons are likely to be found in that molecule.

candidate_cards.front: Compare bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals.
candidate_cards.back: A bonding MO is lower in energy and has electron density between nuclei; an antibonding MO is higher in energy and has a node between nuclei.

candidate_cards.front: What does an additive orbital combination produce?
candidate_cards.back: A lower-energy bonding molecular orbital with electron density between the nuclei.

candidate_cards.front: What does a subtractive orbital combination produce?
candidate_cards.back: A higher-energy antibonding molecular orbital with a node between the nuclei.

candidate_cards.front: Diagram prompt: show pi bonding and pi antibonding MOs for ethylene.
candidate_cards.back: Show same-sign p lobes combining into a filled lower-energy pi bonding MO, and opposite-sign lobes combining into an empty higher-energy pi antibonding MO with a node between carbons.

sections.title: Drawing Chemical Structures
sections.focus: Condensed structures, skeletal structures, implied atoms, and formula counting.
facts: A line between atoms represents the two electrons in a covalent bond.
Condensed structures omit many C-H and C-C single bond lines; groups such as CH3, CH2, and CH imply how many hydrogens are attached.
Parentheses can group repeated substituents, as in (CH3)2 attached to one atom.
In skeletal structures, carbon atoms are normally implied at every line end and line intersection.
Hydrogens bonded to carbon are normally omitted in skeletal structures and supplied mentally to give carbon valence 4.
Atoms other than carbon and hydrogen are normally shown explicitly.
Hydrogens attached to heteroatoms are shown explicitly.
A line end normally represents CH3, a two-way vertex CH2, a three-way vertex CH, and a four-way vertex carbon with no hydrogens, unless multiple bonds or heteroatoms alter the count.

candidate_cards.front: What is a condensed structure?
candidate_cards.back: A shorthand structure where many C-H and C-C single bonds are not drawn but are implied by groups such as CH3, CH2, and CH.

candidate_cards.front: In a skeletal structure, where are carbon atoms implied?
candidate_cards.back: At each line end and at each line intersection, unless an atom is explicitly shown.

candidate_cards.front: Which atoms are usually shown explicitly in skeletal structures?
candidate_cards.back: Atoms other than carbon and hydrogen are shown; hydrogens on heteroatoms are also shown.

candidate_cards.front: A skeletal vertex with two single bonds and no charge or heteroatom label.
candidate_cards.back: It represents a carbon bearing two hydrogens, CH2.

candidate_cards.front: In a simple alkane skeletal drawing, how many hydrogens are on a line-end carbon?
candidate_cards.back: Three hydrogens, so the line-end carbon is CH3.

candidate_cards.front: In a simple alkane skeletal drawing, how many hydrogens are on a four-way carbon vertex?
candidate_cards.back: None; four bonds already fill carbon's usual valence.

candidate_cards.front: Diagram prompt: teach line-angle conventions with one compact example.
candidate_cards.back: Show a skeletal chain and annotate line ends as CH3, two-way vertices as CH2, three-way vertices as CH, heteroatoms as explicit, and omitted carbon-bound hydrogens as implied.
